claims.text: A silicide-based Si-Cr-Fe surface coating can improve the oxidation resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Si, Cr, and Fe are oxidation-resistant alloying elements.
The coating improves oxidation resistance by promoting a dense, adherent protective oxide scale.
The initial substrate is an equimolar MoNbTaTiW refractory high-entropy alloy without additional surface protection.
A Si-20Cr-20Fe coating can be applied to MoNbTaTiW by a fused slurry method.
The coated alloy is subsequently heat treated at approximately 1430 °C.
The high-temperature heat treatment forms silicide phases in the coating.
Processing and subsequent oxidation exposure occur under a controlled inert or vacuum atmosphere.
Protective oxide layers such as chromia or silicide-derived oxides form on top of the coating.
The coating constituents enable in situ formation of a continuous, slow-growing oxide scale.
The oxide scale acts as a diffusion barrier against oxygen ingress.
The oxide scale limits element loss from the coated alloy.
The coated alloy will have a significantly lower high-temperature oxidation rate than an uncoated substrate.
Uncoated refractory high-entropy alloys typically form non-protective oxides and oxidize rapidly.
Coating efficacy varies with substrate composition, coating-process parameters, and operating temperature.
Long-term stability of the protective scale remains to be validated.
The quantitative reduction in oxidation kinetics depends on processing conditions and alloy microstructure.

contradictions.description: The stated subsequent exposure atmosphere is inert or vacuum, while the mechanism and experiment require an oxidation environment with sufficient oxygen ingress to generate measurable oxide-scale growth. The processing atmosphere and oxidation-test atmosphere are not clearly distinguished.
